title: I'm not worried about Fallout: New Vegas 2, because Obsidian knows how to make the best out of a bad situation
author: Fraser Brown
text:
Dungeon Master
(Image credit: Future) Welcome to Dungeon Master , PC Gamer's regular RPG column, where Online Editor Fraser Brown delves into PC gaming's most beloved and enduring genre. Grab a seat in our badly-lit tavern and please ignore the goblin puke.
I have occasionally been accused of cynicism. And by occasionally, I mean every damn day of my life. For this week's Dungeon Master column, however, I am choosing the path of optimism. Specifically, when it comes to Obsidian and its ability to make a great follow up to Fallout: New Vegas , despite everything .
Since 2004, the studio has crafted a litany of exceptional RPGs. Knights of the Old Republic 2, Neverwinter Nights 2, Alpha Protocol, Fallout: New Vegas, South Park: The Stick of Truth, Pillars of Eternity, Tyranny, Pillars of Eternity 2—what an incredible run.
Sure, sandwiched between that lot we got games like Armored Warfare and Skyforge—forgettable detours that kept the lights on—and I'm less enamoured with its later offerings, but Obsidian still has an enviable track record, and for 14 years it felt like it couldn't miss.
Over this period, Obsidian worked with a lot of different publishers, and it never seemed able to find its forever partner. Right from the get-go, things were rocky. LucasArts gave the KotOR 2 team a mere 15 months to develop the highly-anticipated sequel, which seems shocking now, but less so in the early 2000s. Unsurprisingly, it wasn't long enough. The game was delayed, cuts were made, and the game launched in a messy state.
But it was astonishing. Obsidian eschewed the well-trodden path to tell a story that completely recontextualised core Star Wars elements like the Force. If KotOR was Baldur's Gate, KotOR 2 was Planescape: Torment—philosophical, tragic, beautifully written.
It was a challenging beginning for the young studio, and the challenges just kept on coming.
(Image credit: Obsidian) Obsidian seemed to have an easier go of things with Atari and Neverwinter Nights 2. Atari pushed back the deadline to give the team more time, and there was support from BioWare as well. But at the same time it had a project canned by Disney, and then Sega, who Obsidian worked with again on Alpha Protocol, a game that struggled to come together thanks to both the studio and publisher.
Fallout: New Vegas, arguably Obsidian's most celebrated game, had its fair share of troubles.
Despite this, Alpha Protocol still ended up being pretty special. Sales were poor, but it still maintains a cult following—particularly among game journalists. Every year, when we're figuring out the Top 100, Alpha Protocol is in that discussion.
Fallout: New Vegas, arguably Obsidian's most celebrated game, had its fair share of troubles, too. Bethesda gave Obsidian only 18 months to develop the RPG—the studio's largest and most ambitious project to date. The tight deadline and the team's inexperience with Bethesda's tech, specifically the Gamebryo engine, led to an extremely janky game at launch—to the point where it was fundamentally broken in parts. There was also a significant amount of cut content.
Its success, then, was impressive. It's often touted as the best of the Bethesda-era Fallouts, or the best Fallout ever, which feels like a fair assessment. Its glaring flaws, however, could not be overlooked by everyone, netting the game a Metacritic score that wasn't quite high enough to earn the developers a bonus from Bethesda.
(Image credit: Bethesda) After failing to talk Atari into giving it enough money to make Baldur's Gate 3, Obsidian took matters into its own hands and Kickstarted Pillars of Eternity—an Infinity Engine love letter. It was make or break for the studio, which was close to bankruptcy. It pulled through. The campaign was a huge success, and Pillars lived up to the studio's promises.
Paradox Interactive was the publisher this time, and the pair would work on one more project together, Tyranny, before they had a slightly awkward breakup. Sadly, Tyranny's story remains incomplete. It wasn't designed to stand alone, but hopes of a sequel were swiftly crushed. Then we got Pillars of Eternity 2: Deadfire, another crowdfunded CRPG. It's Obsidian's best CRPG, hands down, but it sold poorly.
This led to some soul searching at Obsidian. Because both games in the series were crowdfunded, Obsidian was determined to give players what they said they wanted. Indeed, Josh Sawyer called Pillars of Eternity and its sequel "the most compromised games" he'd ever worked on , because backers wanted an Infinity Engine-style game, which meant he had to accept "bad designed decisions" in the name of nostalgia. And it worked for Pillars 1, so why not Deadfire?
Basically, Obsidian couldn't figure out what went wrong. Were CRPGs dead again? Did people just not care about sequels? The imminent arrival and astronomical success of Disco Elysium and Baldur's Gate 3 suggested this wasn't the case. One thing was clear, though: Obsidian needed to "re-examine the entire format" of the series.
(Image credit: Obsidian Entertainment) Now we've arrived in the Microsoft era. Obsidian was acquired by Xbox—an incredibly weird fit—at the end of 2018. And then we got The Outer Worlds—a game that, despite its polish, felt a lot more stuck in the past than its isometric CRPGs. It was fine. It had all the ingredients one would expect from an Obsidian RPG. But it seemed to be missing the secret sauce. It didn't feel ambitious or weird, and storytelling-wise it was a massive step back.
Something had definitely changed.
Most of the people who made Obsidian this great studio were still around. Microsoft's massacre was still years away. But something had definitely changed. Avowed followed, and we finally got to see the product of Obsidian's re-examination of Pillars of Eternity.
Avowed's journey to launch is fascinating, and in hindsight feels like pretty clear evidence that Obsidian had lost confidence after Deadfire. Avowed was initially pitched as a multiplayer game: a first-person, open-world fantasy romp like The Elder Scrolls, but with a Destiny-style multiplayer component. Microsoft seemed to like it so much they bought the entire studio, but the multiplayer element was ditched.
If you cast your mind back to 2024, you might recall how worried Obsidian had become about the Skyrim comparisons. Basically, every single time someone from Obsidian discussed Avowed, they tried to make it very clear that it wasn't doing its own take on The Elder Scrolls (despite that being the initial pitch). Which was reasonable, in that Obsidian definitely did not make something that felt like Skyrim. But it was also hard not to read this as nervousness.
(Image credit: Obsidian Entertainment) Instead, Obsidian said, it was a fantasy take on The Outer Worlds. Which probably seemed like a safe bet. The Outer Worlds has never garnered the love enjoyed by a lot of its earlier games, but it was a commercial success. Trying to fit a Pillars game into that mould probably sounded sensible, if conservative. Unfortunately, Avowed was neither a commercial success or a big hit critically—though it wasn't particularly badly received either. It did OK.
The Outer Worlds was popular enough to receive a sequel, and while Obsidian's second outing in that universe improved on the first, the writing, the characters, the world building—it all felt like a studio trying to copy Obsidian, and more specifically Fallout, but failing to capture what made its previous games special.
Somehow, a survival game, Grounded, and a narrative adventure, Pentiment, have ended up being the best games of the Microsoft era so far. Despite the genres not being in Obsidian's traditional wheelhouse, they still seemed to capture the old magic.
With Grounded, it was the world building, and the setting in general—not only was it fun and inventive, it tied everything together beautifully. And with Pentiment, it was all about the characters and writing. Sharp, funny, starting from a point where there's an assumption that players are smart enough to vibe with a wordy ecclesiastical mystery.
(Image credit: Microsoft) These games were evidence that Obsidian was still full of talented designers. So what went wrong with the RPGs? The Outer Worlds in particular should have been an unmitigated slam dunk. Tim Cain and Leonard Boyarsky had returned, and there'd been this hope that RPG fans would be dining on something just as brilliant as Fallout. But it never happened.
These games were evidence that Obsidian was still full of talented designers.
Is Microsoft to blame? That would be an easy answer, but one that doesn't hold up to much scrutiny. The Outer Worlds was already in development when the acquisition began. Was it the team's lack of familiarity with Unreal Engine 4? Probably not. Obsidian's last few RPGs have been a lot more polished than its usual fare, and by Avowed and The Outer Worlds 2, both Unreal Engine 5 games, it had plenty of experience.
I'm increasingly convinced that it's a rut brought on by the studio's inability to figure out why Deadfire didn't set the world ablaze. It's certainly what led to Avowed, but it sure seems like The Outer Worlds is a product of the studio's growing doubts. There's also the hint of a midlife crisis. Obsidian is pretty old, remember. It was founded 23 years ago, but really it's even older than that, spawning as it did out of Black Isle.
So how does it get out of this rut? Condensing its 23-year-history into an article like this, it does look a bit like bouncing from project to project, skirting bankruptcy, and navigating the weird demands and expectations of myriad publishers pushed Obsidian into making its best games. But this explanation—that Obsidian does its best work when everything is on fire—leaves a bad taste in the mouth.
(Image credit: Obsidian) I want to make one thing very clear: Microsoft's apocalyptic ravaging of the videogame industry is reprehensible. It swallowed up a bunch of studios it had no idea what to do with, and now the devs are being punished for Microsoft's mismanagement. I hate that Obsidian staff got a tiny taste of job security and then had it mercilessly snatched away. It absolutely sucks.
If this was any other studio, I'm not sure it could survive losing a quarter of its employees before being tasked with developing a sequel to its most ambitious and celebrated RPG. But this is Obsidian. For 23 years, it's been relentlessly screwed over by publishers and still managed to put out some of the best RPGs ever made.
So it would be ghoulish to suggest that the layoffs and instability will improve Obsidian. And bullshit, too. You don't make a good game by firing a bunch of talent. But Obsidian is a survivor. It takes shitty situations and makes gold.
And I'm pretty sure New Vegas 2 is its best chance of doing that. It's got the talent and the experience, and for most of the last decade it's essentially been trying to do its own Fallout with The Outer Worlds. And while there are a lot of things I dislike about The Outer Worlds and its sequel, I think it really boils down to one thing: these games want to be Fallout, but they're not. It's like the uncanny valley effect—their proximity to Fallout showed up all the ways in which they weren't as good as Fallout.
(Image credit: Wizards of the Coast, Bethesda) Obsidian has earned grace and faith. As critical as I am regarding its last trio of RPGs, how can I not feel at least somewhat confident that it can knock New Vegas 2 out of the park?
So I truly think the studio will rise to the occasion. Obsidian knows how to make a good Fallout, Josh Sawyer knows how to make a good Fallout. It's trapped in a relationship with one of the scummiest publishers around, it's lost a lot of talent, and after this month's massacre I think everything Xbox-related will be irrevocably tainted. But Obsidian has been set up to fail several times before, and it frequently manages to surprise us.

I want to make one thing very clear: Microsoft's apocalyptic ravaging of the videogame industry is reprehensible. It swallowed up a bunch of studios it had no idea what to do with, and now the devs are being punished for Microsoft's mismanagement. I hate that Obsidian staff got a tiny taste of job security and then had it mercilessly snatched away. It absolutely sucks.

If this was any other studio, I'm not sure it could survive losing a quarter of its employees before being tasked with developing a sequel to its most ambitious and celebrated RPG. But this is Obsidian. For 23 years, it's been relentlessly screwed over by publishers and still managed to put out some of the best RPGs ever made.

So it would be ghoulish to suggest that the layoffs and instability will improve Obsidian. And bullshit, too. You don't make a good game by firing a bunch of talent. But Obsidian is a survivor. It takes shitty situations and makes gold.

And I'm pretty sure New Vegas 2 is its best chance of doing that. It's got the talent and the experience, and for most of the last decade it's essentially been trying to do its own Fallout with The Outer Worlds. And while there are a lot of things I dislike about The Outer Worlds and its sequel, I think it really boils down to one thing: these games want to be Fallout, but they're not. It's like the uncanny valley effect—their proximity to Fallout showed up all the ways in which they weren't as good as Fallout.

Obsidian has earned grace and faith. As critical as I am regarding its last trio of RPGs, how can I not feel at least somewhat confident that it can knock New Vegas 2 out of the park?

So I truly think the studio will rise to the occasion. Obsidian knows how to make a good Fallout, Josh Sawyer knows how to make a good Fallout. It's trapped in a relationship with one of the scummiest publishers around, it's lost a lot of talent, and after this month's massacre I think everything Xbox-related will be irrevocably tainted. But Obsidian has been set up to fail several times before, and it frequently manages to surprise us.

title: I used videogames to solve my country's politics: Turns out the answer is ultra-mega-communism
author: Joshua Wolens
text:
The country I lead is in uproar. My approval ratings have to be measured on entirely new axes to capture popular upset. The streets throng with rebels and malcontents. The only reason I have not been assassinated is that the sheer number of people who want to murder me cannot fit through the door at the same time.
The election takes place tomorrow. The situation is excellent.
(Image credit: Positech Games) The United Kingdom is in a parlous state (I'm talking about real life now). The current Labour prime minister—who I will not name because that's simply not information any of us will ever need again—has resigned and a new one, former Manchester mayor Andy Burnham, is imminent. Based largely on vibes and the fact Burnham has a northern accent, the British elite is girding itself for hyper-Bolshevism. How will the nation fare under our imminent war communist regime?
I can answer that. Using cutting edge models (a copy of political sim Democracy 4 ), I have exhaustively plotted out the trajectory of a radical premiership in an exacting replica of the UK in 2026. Friends, I've cracked it. My advanced technologies have revealed exactly what course Britain's prime minister should take. Join me as I walk you through it.
What is to be done?
Of course, to accurately foresee the possible political trajectories of the UK, my simulation needs to reflect the country as it is. The British Isles are a peculiar beast, and capturing them in simulation means I need to be able to make a variety of fine-tuned adjustments.
(Image credit: Positech Games) Fortunately, Democracy 4:
Lets you simply choose the UK as a country to run from a list of options.
Lets you tweak it a little bit before you hit the road.
Per YouGov polling, the British public considers itself +15% liberal-leaning and +3% socialist-leaning, which I duly reflected in Democracy's settings. The national debt—a made-up number the Treasury invents to give the chancellor something to talk about in meetings—is around £3 trillion. Into the simulator it goes.
But it wasn't quite enough. This might be my home country numerically , but the spirit wasn't there—I had detail without soul. The sine qua non of British politics was missing. Some subtle, herbal ingredient was absent.
It came to me. I named all three main parties The Fascists and gave them different-coloured rosettes.
(Image credit: Positech Games) Nationalised sausages
My UK simulacrum—simUKlacrum—was mostly perfect. The skies were grey, the people dour, the spending high, the income low, the bourgeois revolution frustratingly incomplete. The only thing that seemed off was that my party—the Burnham crew—inexplicably had 10 million members and climbing. If I woke up tomorrow and heard that 10 million people had joined any UK political party I would immediately flee the country.
Apart from that? All verisimilitudinous : a true-to-life canvas on which to etch the social revolution. I decided my first move would be to try to bring that debt down—bringing expenditure below spending by waging a merciless Red Terror on the City of London and military-industrial complex.
(Image credit: Positech Games) We started as we meant to go on: boldly. Democracy 4 tasks you with balancing ministers' loyalty and their capability when selecting your cabinet. You might have troops who would go to war for you, but who would be useless at implementing your policies, or vice versa. Both are important.
I completely disregarded this and filled every post with the most obedient stooges I had to hand. Then we got to work.
The UK nuclear arsenal? Abolished. The military? Reduced to five of England's reddest dads. Corporation tax went up, capital gains had their pockets turned out; the nation's wealthy were a tube of delicious tomato paste and I was the chef de partie.
Shark-infested waters
International capital was not happy with this turn of events. The UK credit rating tumbled down a cliff face and smashed its head into every rock along the way: AAA became AA became BB became CCC became C—the ruling class was mashing the keyboard to register its displeasure, as meanwhile rivals took advantage of our newly hamstrung defences.
(Image credit: Positech Games) Argentina planted a flag on the Falklands, Russian ships drifted alarmingly close to the coast. At one point pirates manifested. I had implemented socialism in one country with such forceful enthusiasm I had somehow returned us to the Age of Sail.
None of this particularly bothered me. Let credit agencies toss entire cans of alphabetti spaghetti at me, let Argentina call them Las Malvinas. If Russia wants to paddle menacingly in our waters I'll just add it to the yearly tourism stats. Pirates are fun!
What did bother me was that the British public wasn't too psyched about how things were going either. I had come into office with unenviable approval polling and my moves to reshape the national finances along more egalitarian lines had only made things worse. Though, hilariously, I never polled as badly as the actual, real-life Labour Party, things were nonetheless on a downward trend. Even more galling: expenditure still outpaced income to the tune of £15 billion or so.
(Image credit: Positech Games) I consulted my advisers—a YouTube clip of Limmy saying don't back down, double down—and decided the answer was to become even more radically communist than I had been previously.
The five-turn plan
We needed new policies, not just tweaks to the old one. I began by implementing city farms: new kolkhozes to feed a hungry people as their fortress weathers capitalist assault.
I went further. We banned cryptocurrency, subsidised healthy food, handed out university grants to anyone who showed interest in buying a book, and taxed employers who used AI. Inflation spiralled and expenditure climbed, but my polling stabilised. Britain did not love me, but its hatred stopped growing.
Then two things happened which turned things around. First, I legislated the right to die. Britain loved this. They went absolutely nuts for it, as though they had been waiting around for someone to tell them they could die for decades. My polling shot through the roof. By which I mean it entered the general vicinity of 43% or so.
(Image credit: Positech Games) Shortly after, the whole credit rating and inflation scenario got so bad that parliament declared a state of emergency. Paradoxically, this meant I—the guy who had very much caused all this—now had way more power and political capital than I did before. I went hogwild with it. I created a state postal service and dragged its slider all the way to the right: maximum postal service . State airlines got the same treatment, as did the NHS, which now had sufficient annual income to cure death.
I also embarked on a bold policy of 'giving everyone free money,' which was popular. All of this was well-timed: the election was now imminent.
All power to the soviets
Here we come full circle, right back to where I started this piece. Britain was a nation cut in two. Socialists, trade unionists, and the poor (all of which are actual, modelled voter groups in Democracy 4) loved me. Meanwhile, in the blue corner, religious conservatives and capitalists had become so outraged at my leadership they had begun to create armed paramilitaries with names like "The Angels of Heavenly Justice."
The question was: who could better mobilise at the ballot box? Also, could I make it to the election without some modern-day Fanny Kaplan taking my head off with a light machine gun?
(Image credit: Positech Games) I hit the campaign trail with the aim of infuriating my enemies even further. There would be no rapprochement, no outreach, no olive branch to my foes. I had no interest in winning over floating voters or in persuading anyone who was not firmly in the tank already. Every speech I gave had the goal of inciting my followers to a spittle-flecked fever pitch. Meanwhile, I focused my campaign on slandering my opponents.
Somehow, it worked. 70% of my base turned out to put an X next to my name, while my nearest competitors barely managed 46%. The result was that, on a nationwide turnout of 72%, I came away with 30 million votes (or 44.7% overall), completely blowing my reactionary foes out of the water.
Britain's credit was in the tank, Russia was on the verge of seizing Kent, and buying a loaf of bread required one of those duffel bags full of cash they have in Heat, but the people were with me. I had been re-elected. The red dawn brings a bright new day.
(Image credit: Positech Games) Feel the burn
What can we take from this? In real life, Britain will soon get its new prime minister, and the compromises have already begun. Many of the faces and ideas that surrounded the outgoing, now-despised PM are already reappearing.
(Image credit: Positech Games) Clearly, this is doomed. As my rigorous testing has proved, what 21st century Britain needs is a sweeping cavalcade of courageous policies. We need collective farms, punitive taxes, the immediate execution of anyone with a business studies qualification. Bold, radical action—this is what science says this green and pleasant land requires.
That is, if you want to win the next election. I guess if not then, hey, just keep doing whatever.
Mr Burnham, I'm just a phone call away.

title: Raids just landed in solo 'simulated MMO' Erenshor
author: Justin Wagner
text:
If hell is other people, heaven might just be Erenshor—assuming you like old-school MMOs in the style of EverQuest, anyway. It's very much that style of game, but in a simulated solo world where other 'players' are just computer-controlled NPCs called simplayers. You can even party up and form a guild with them, which will come in handy now that raids are live.
They arrived last Monday in the Planar March patch, and solo developer Brian of Burgee Media called it "the biggest day for Erenshor since its launch" in the Steam community release blog .
"When I promised raids I had no idea how the heck I was going to implement it. It sort of hung over my head like an intimidating shadow until I finally dove into it," he wrote. "With the help of the amazing community of testers, all of your feedback, and a few really late nights, it's here!"
There are four raid zones, as well as 21 new bosses to kill in exchange for fat loots. You can create raid teams in the guild menu and they'll automatically join when you start the instance—no stopping to wait for someone to pay the pizza guy or head back to a capital city so they can repair all their broken gear, I imagine.
As a lifelong MMO casual who struggles to make time for raid night, this sounds like a dream come true simply for the convenience factor. I do wonder how Erenshor will retain the difficulty and sense of scale you get in an online raid without making you wrangle several dozen real people's schedules and manually ensure they all know what their class does, but considering this is based on the pre-World of Warcraft world of MMOs, I'm sure there's plenty of glorious grinding and dying in store anyway.
It seems like Erenshor has found a hungry audience for its simulated world. You can buy it on Steam , where it sits at a "very positive" rating with 94% of user reviews recommending the game.

title: Amazon's God of War TV show will recast Kratos due to on-set injury
author: Justin Wagner
text:
Remember that photo which stirred all sorts of talk about Amazon's upcoming God of War TV series? Well, the show won't look like that anymore—the role of Kratos is set to be recast since actor Ryan Hurst tore a bicep on set, according to Deadline . Anonymous sources in that story claim Hurst has had surgery and is recovering.
As Deadline points out, this comes after Hurst "underwent a physical transformation" and put on 40 pounds of muscle specifically to play Kratos. But for such a physical role and with a child actor (who's in every scene with the character, one assumes) to consider, it seems starting over is the simplest way forward for Amazon.
Production paused right after the injury and is planned to restart by mid-October with someone new in the role. In other words, any scenes that have already been shot will have to be redone—with four episodes already wrapped, that's a huge reset. After a mixed reaction to that initial photo, Hurst won't get the chance to prove his naysayers wrong in the end.
Hurst is also in Christopher Nolan's new Odyssey movie as Mentor, and theater-avoidant gamers may know him as Thor in God of War: Ragnarok or Beta in AMC's Walking Dead series. It's not clear who will take his place, but given the reported production schedule, we won't be waiting long to find out.
Setbacks aside, at least the show will be easier to experience on your PC than God of War Laufey, which seems likely to forego the PC .

title: Grab a free Steam game full of misery and decision-making for a limited time
author: Jody Macgregor
text:
In 2021, when The Life and Suffering of Sir Brante came out on Steam, our Shaun Prescott called it "a text heavy narrative RPG with a huge emphasis on gruelling decision making." Think of those decision-heavy simulations like Princess Maker, only in a grim-and-gritty fantasy setting that cranks up the George R. R. Martin dial to max.
"Step into the harsh world of the Blessed Arknian Empire and experience the life of Sir Brante," as the announcement puts it, "a man born into a rigid society where every choice matters and every decision carries consequences. Shape your destiny through years of struggle, ambition, sacrifice, and suffering in this narrative RPG, where your actions determine not only your own fate but also the fate of those around you."
The Life and Suffering of Sir Brante is free to keep on Steam until July 23 to promote the upcoming release of a new game in the same setting, The Life and Suffering of Prince Jerian , which casts you in the role of a crown prince, born to a life of political intrigue. A whole new flavor of suffering to enjoy.

title: Stardew Valley comes to Magic: The Gathering and fans aren't taking some of the new artwork well
author: Jody Macgregor
text:
The limited releases of cards for Magic: The Gathering that are mostly reskins of existing cards with new art are called Secret Lair drops. They're infamous for selling out fast and being hard to get hold of at normal prices, and they're also infamous for having unusual themes. There's been a Monty Python one , a Dwarf Fortress one , and even a Garfield one . Next? Stardew Valley.
ConcernedApe's quirky farm-life sim has a legion of dedicated fans who have built their own mimetic lore on top of the actual story of the game, like Overwatch stans interpreting and shipping characters in ways Blizzard didn't intend. Take Elliott, for instance, a sentimental writer who lives on the beach and is among Stardew Valley's romanceable cast. According to fan artists, he's a willowy bishonen boy. According to ConcernedApe's own art for the Mermaid's Pendant card, a reskin of the existing Wedding Ring card, he's a square-jawed Chad.

They've called him a "Habbo hotel looking mf" and roasted his "Sheriff Woody lookin’ ass". He's been compared to Matt Smith's character in House of the Dragon, Fabio, and a member of the famously inbred House of Hapsburg, while others declare "We have Elliot at home" and say "I might have to marry Alex now."
Other cards show Penny with ringlets rather than the buns players assumed she had based on the in-game art, and depict Leah as substantially thicker than you might have assumed she would be. ConcernedApe's illustrations in particular have always been a bit on the "programmer art" end of the spectrum, from the moment you see grandpa's odd-looking bed at the start of the game. title: Every new Pal in Palworld 1.0 and where to catch them
author: Andrea Shearon
text:
The Palworld 1.0 update adds 72 new pals—most of which you can catch, while the remainder at least adds an updated entry to your Palpedia. That's a big undertaking with the expanded Palpagos map and the new World Tree region to explore, and referencing the in-game map can be a real pain, but that's where I come in to hopefully make the process a bit easier.
How to catch every new pal in Palworld 1.0
This list was made to highlight where you're most likely to encounter the new 1.0 pals for the first time, but some spawn in more than one region. Pals that pop up in multiple locations will have a note indicating other places you can find them, but are only listed once to keep the process simple.
The level recommendations don't account for bosses in the region, so keep that in mind before you go barreling into their arena. Some zones are harder or easier to catch new pals in depending on terrain obstacles and gear, so take them as loose guidelines—not hard and fast rules.
A few tips to start collecting all 72 new pals
Make sure to catch five of every pal for bonus XP and a Mimog Effigy.
Use the Pal Tamer's Glasses, Ring of Mercy, or a pal with Mercy Hit so wild pals don't drop below 1 HP before you can catch them.
Think you have enough Pal Spheres? Wrong . Catching multiple of each pal for bonuses or better passives meant I never had enough, so keep stocking up.

title: 007: First Light was originally going to be less about James Bond and more of 'an ensemble piece', with 'all the 00s working together, as they do in Slovakia'
author: Rick Lane
text:
hen I played 007: First Light earlier this year, one element of it stood out to me as unusual—and that is the arc relating to Bond's fellow 00 trainees, Cressida Bright and Lennox Monroe. IO Interactive puts a huge amount of work into building these characters, successfully selling you on the inherently bizarre concept of James Bond having flatmates.
Yet just as you warm to these characters, they vanish from the story, and after MI6's failed operation to eliminate the rogue 009 in Slovakia, Bond primarily teams up with his mentor, Greenway.
All of this is well portrayed. But the cadence of it nonetheless struck me as odd while playing. It turns out there might be a reason for this. IO Interactive initially intended for First Light to be less squarely focused on Bond, while his pals would have played a much bigger role in the story.
Speaking to Eurogamer , First Light's lead writer Michael Vogt explained how the game's first act came together. "During the training sequence, we make a false promise," Vogt said. "Basically, we're saying 'This is going to be an ensemble piece, all the 00s working together, as they do in Slovakia'.
"And then we pull the rug out from under you when most of them die, and serendipitously, [Bond's], the last man standing. He could have died in that explosion but he doesn't, and so he emerges as the top agent. But in my very first pitch I think we were actually toying with the idea of making it an ensemble piece, that you had the different agents working together."
Logically, this makes sense. You're not going to put a newly trained agent out in the field on their own until you're certain they can handle it, which given Bond's roguish tendencies would probably take a while. But IO ultimately cut the ensemble concept short to kickstart Bond's character development.
"The story beat that it serves is of course that it goes from all fun and games for him—he's a young kid, he's on an adventure, and he's out globetrotting and playing secret agent—but after that explosion, he wakes up to the harsh reality. When M says that [00] life expectancy is very short, it's like 'Oh, right''. He gets it, and he matures from that, of course, and also from the guilt—maybe the survivor's guilt—of being the one who made it."
Vogt can't recall when exactly this change was made, but it would explain why Cressida and Monroe feel so much like companions who are going to accompany Bond through the entire game. For at least a part of the game's development, that was the plan.

title: 'GTA 6 needs this': This GTA 5 prison mod turns one of roleplay's most enduring staples into a game within a game
author: Joe Donnelly
text:
I still remember cursing aloud when I was first sent to prison in GTA 5 roleplay.
You see, unlike in regular Grand Theft Auto—story mode or Online—getting arrested in RP has consequences . Sure, you face the same trigger-happy cops when you fall foul of the law, where you're pursued until either dead or in cuffs, and are then hit with the same 'Wasted' or 'Busted' mandates depending on the outcome of the chase. Assuming the latter transpires, however, you don't simply receive a fine and a reset wanted star meter—in the majority of GTA RP servers, you instead respawn in the Bolingbroke penitentiary.
The magnitude of your crime determines the length of your stay as you pace around the recreation ground doing everything you can to avoid contact with anyone else, lest you find yourself punching lumps out of one another and extending your stay. Now, XmanStudios has introduced the whole ordeal to GTA 5 singleplayer by way of their mod, Jailbreak .
"Jailbreak is a GTA 5 script that adds a prison sentence system to singleplayer," reads the mod's description. "If the player dies or gets arrested while wanted, they are transported to Bolingbroke Penitentiary and must serve a sentence based on the wanted level they had at the time.
"The current version includes prison bus transport, prison processing, prisoner outfits, sentence timers, cell entrance and exit markers, lockdown triggers, guard reactions, baton-based cell returns, and basic escape behaviour. During normal prison time, guards and prisoners roam around the prison. If the player causes trouble, enters restricted areas, or tries to escape, the prison can enter lockdown and guards will respond."
Through all of that, players can expect visible cell entrance and exit markers, a prison lockdown system, restricted area lockdown triggers and a brutally violent so-called 'baton-based return-to-cell system' which leaves very little to the imagination. Updates in recent weeks include basic jailbreaking features, such as Shawshank Redemption-style digging, bed dummies and stealth mechanics that only kick into gear after lights out.
A quick glance at the mod page's comments reveals the warm reception Jailbreak has received so far (a few weeks on from launch and it's cracked 3,000 downloads), however there is one that immediately caught my eye. Crazyboy4881 says: "GTA 6 NEEDS THIS." And, given the prominence of prison in the scant snatches we've seen so far of the next Grand Theft Auto adventure, I really couldn't agree more.

title: Gears of War's creator is considering returning to game development, but whatever he makes won't be PvP like his last efforts: 'Good luck to anyone in that space'
author: Rick Lane
text:
Eight years after leaving the games industry, Gears of War creator Cliff Bleszinski is considering a full-time return to game development.
Bleszinski left the games industry in 2018 after the closure of his studio Boss Key Productions , caused by the commercial failure of its two games—the multiplayer arena shooter LawBreakers , and the '80s-themed Battle Royale game Radical Heights . At the time, Bleszinski swore off making games forever .
Yet now, in a wide-ranging interview with 80 Level , Bleszinski explained that's considering coming back. In the chat, Bleszinski discussed the events of his life since leaving the games industry, during which he wrote an autobiography , produced a Tony award-winning musical , and faced up to a long struggle with alcoholism.
The latter resulted in Bleszinski being hospitalised in March this year, in the aftermath of which he gave up drinking. It's been during his sobriety that Bleszinski says he rediscovered his love for games—and the desire to make them:
"At the end of the day, I want to create characters and worlds," Bleszinski explained to journalist Brian Crecente. "I want to make stuff that people will cosplay and get tattooed on their bodies."
Bleszinski has already returned to game development in an advisory role—having consulted on a horror game called Soul Walker . This experience appears to have been positive for him, as he's now pondering a full-time comeback. "So maybe I'll eventually get my full foot back in the business and hopefully not get pushed into the pool."
Bleszinski didn't go into detail about what kind of game he wants to make during the interview. But he did discuss what he won't be making, namely PvP multiplayer games like those created by Boss Key:
"Good luck to anyone in that space," he said. "I'm more of a fan of PvE these days. Horde mode saved Gears 2, and I believe that space is evergreen because players just want to hop online with friends and shoot some stuff, no frills, no questions asked."
Nonetheless, it seems like Bleszinski has an idea he wants to pursue, even if he didn't vocalise it. "I'm nowhere near sharing anything specific (about a new game), beyond that, I can't walk into a Home Depot without seeing a full arsenal at every turn," he said, adding that "There's so much more than just chainsaws."
PvP or not, I'd certainly be up for playing a new Bleszinski-led game. While LawBreakers failed to find an audience, as a multiplayer shooter it was thoroughly entertaining. Radical Heights had promise too, though it never got a chance to develop into something substantial.
Of course, I'd be most interested in a spiritual successor to Gears. That space has been left fallow for a long time, and Pragmata recently showed there's a big appetite for that style of game. But all of this is contingent on whether Bleszinski actually comes back, which isn't guaranteed. In 2020, Bleszinski said he felt an urge to make "a little game". But for whatever reason that didn't transpire, at least not publicly.

title: God of War Laufey star Deborah Ann Woll isn't phased by the negative reactions to its announcement: 'I feel totally unbothered'
author: Rick Lane
text:
In a depressingly predictable turn of events, the reveal God of War Laufey came under fire from certain corners of the Internet, as it centres around a female protagonist rather than mad lad turned sad dad Kratos.
Much of this negative reaction has centred around Laufey's actor Deborah Ann Woll, who also played Laufey in the 2018 reboot. But Woll, who also plays Karen Page in Marvel's Daredevil and its reboot Daredevil: Born Again, isn't phased by the impotent rage of misogynistic online trolls:
Woll was asked about the backlash to the game's reveal by TikTok influencer quinnphobic at Florida Supercon (via Eurogamer ) who recorded the actor's response for TikTok :
"Genuinely, I thought I was going to be much more affected by it, but one, I'm not on social media, so that helps, and two, I don't know, I feel totally unbothered," Woll replied. "Because I just know it's great. It's okay if it's not your cup of tea, but in no universe is it bad."
I'll admit to being surprised by Sony Santa Monica's direction for the next God of War , since Kratos has been at the centre of it since the very beginning. But having watched the lengthy reveal trailer/game demo, you can hardly say it isn't in the spirit of the franchise. The idea of carving my way through the afterlife with a big wobbly cube companion seems rad, and if anything, Laufey is truer to the series' original design philosophy than the more recent reboots, returning to a more traditional combat system
I felt like the Norse setting had run its course by the end of God of War: Ragnarök , and some new blood was needed for the series to continue. Besides, Sony Santa Monica has said that Kratos will return in future games anyway . So why be mad? Of course, we know why some people are mad, and it has nothing to do with the quality of the game.
What I will be mad at, however, is if God of War Laufey doesn't come to PC. Both God of War and Ragnarök saw a delayed PC release after Sony discovered that launching its PlayStation exclusives on Steam et al is like printing money . But in May, Sony said it is retreating from the PC as a platform as it recommits to PlayStation exclusives being, well, exclusive.
This would suggest that Laufey will be stuck on PS5 (or possibly PS6 by the time it launches). Personally, though, I don't see this decision lasting all that long. PC is just too big a platform to ignore nowadays, and games like Laufey are so expensive to make that they need as wide a distribution as possible to succeed.

title: 'The mid-2000s was the golden era of first-person shooters': David Szymanski, creator of Dusk and Iron Lung, discusses the games on his PC
author: Rick Lane
text:
Disk Cleanup
(Image credit: Future) Welcome to Disk Cleanup , our regular weekend feature delving into the PCs of PC gaming luminaries. Come back every weekend to read a new interview, digging into the important questions, like "How tidy is your desktop?" and "What game will you never uninstall?"
David Szymanski, creator of Dusk and one of the chief architects of the retro FPS revival, grew up playing games like Lemmings and Oil's Well on the family PC. Among these family favourites was a formative first-person game. But it probably isn't the one you'd expect: "The most foundational one I can remember is playing Myst for the first time," says the New Blood designer. "That was the first game I remember really getting super into—being able to enter another world and explore it in first-person."
Initially a designer of short horror games, Szymanski's breakout came in 2018 with Dusk, an homage to classic '90s shooters like Doom and Quake . Following Dusk's success, Szymanski returned to developing shorter games, including the hit submarine horror game Iron Lung, which was adapted into a movie by YouTuber Markiplier earlier this year.
Szymanski's current project is different from everything else he's made, an isometric game called B.U.G.B.I.T.E which is still in its early stages and is yet to be formally announced: "The only consistency I have is that I keep changing what I'm doing", he says. "I haven't figured out a good, succinct way to pitch it to people because it's not a very complicated game, but it also kind of is at the same time."
Szymanski took a break from blasting bugs as we delved into the fathomless blood ocean of his Steam library, a journey that took us from the apex of survival games to the most obscure corners of the FPS.
What game are you currently playing?
(Image credit: Newtonic Studio, Digital Spray Studios) I am playing an old FPS called Instinct from 2007. It's one of those slavjank games. I got it in the Ultimate Slavjank Collection Bundle on Steam, and I just happened to see a video about it the other day, and was like "Oh, that seems up my alley". It's [on] the same engine as You Are Empty.
It's a pretty simple, barebones FPS, very much like You Are Empty. I don't think it's the same developer, but it's the same engine, so it has the same very hard to explain feel. The way the weapons recoil, the way enemies ragdoll and everything … you don't even have a run button.
You just kind of walk through these very linear Russian science facility hallways. Is it Russian? I don't even know where it's set because half the cutscenes don't work for me. I only have the most tentative grasp on the story … but it's not a very complicated story. There's a facility. There's zombies. You go in and shoot the zombies, and there's also evil guys with guns who you also shoot.
There's something very approachable about it. We have a huge variety of different kinds of FPS right now, but it's a bit of a novelty to have a FPS that's simple and slow and not highly technical …. Although I'm very much a boomer-shooter fan, and of course am known for Dusk, I would say that the mid-2000s was the golden era of first-person shooters, just in terms of the sheer number and variety that we had. It was after all games were Doom clones, but it was before all games were Call of Duty 4 clones.
There wasn't really this codified—or COD-ified—design for what a shooter was supposed to look like … you had Serious Sam a few years earlier, Painkiller a few years earlier. You had Halo doing its own thing. You had Half-Life 2 doing its own thing. You had Doom 3 and Far Cry , just this huge variety of different things that had all sorts of different mechanics and ways of interacting with it.
I've always considered, like, the '90s, maybe you would call it the silver age. And then I think late '90s early to mid-2000s is your golden age of FPSs. And then we enter the brown age.
What was the previous game you played, and is it still installed?
(Image credit: Endnight Games) The previous games that I was mainlining was The Forest , which I never played when it came out because I didn't consider myself a big survival crafting person. Now I'm wondering if maybe I do like survival crafting games when they have goals, because I loved Subnautica and I love The Forest.
However, I haven't finished either of them, not because either of them are bad, but because I have—how many hours do I have in the Forest? 20 exactly. That's about my cutoff point attention-wise. That's the time where I go "I'd really like to finish this, but boy am I feeling like I want to do something new and different." So, it's sitting there waiting for me to go back and finish it. I have failed to finish games that I would consider some of the best things I've ever played. It sucks because that keeps me from being able to enjoy most CRPGs, even though I always enjoy them.
What game did I finish last? Oh, Pragmata ! Which I also loved. That one is still installed because haven't 100%-ed it yet. That was great. I think that's my game of the year so far. It's not a wildly revolutionary thing. It's just crazy to play a AAA game in 2026 that is a short, singleplayer, campaign-driven game with some innovation in the mechanics.
And wouldn't you look at my playtime? Almost exactly 20 hours.
What is the oldest game (by release date) currently installed on your PC?
(Image credit: Id Software) It's got to be Doom. Technically what's installed is the most recent port, but it's still Doom.
I consider Doom to be nearly, objectively, the best FPS ever made. And that's from a combination of historical importance—obviously it's extremely important—and relevance today. You can still go back and play Doom and almost everyone is going to have a good time.
Even if you compare it to Wolfenstein 3D, which is fun in its own way, it has not aged as well as Doom has. And Quake has a lot of improvements, but in some ways does not have the same life to it that Doom does.
I think chaos in vision and game design can actually be a very good thing.
It's a little bit similar to why I think Resident Evil is such an enduring franchise … where it's goofy, it's horror, but it's also action, and it's all of these different things, and as a result you can't really ruin it. And I think it's similar with Doom. In the past, Doom 3 got flak, and Doom 64 got flak. But you can make Doom a little more horror and it still pretty much works. You can make Doom goofier and it still pretty much works. It's such a chaotic mixture of things that it's very hard to actually ruin it.
What is the highest number of hours you have in any given game, according to Steam?
(Image credit: Valve) My play time in games is low compared to most people. The most number of hours I have in anything on Steam is Counter-Strike 2 , because it was formerly Global Offensive, for a whopping 324 hours. But we go down the list … number four is the first singleplayer one, and I wanted to bring this up because it's Elden Ring for 186 hours.
That is exponentially the most time I've ever spent playing through a game, and funnily enough, I love Elden Ring, but I wouldn't say it's necessarily on my top 10 list. It'd be on my top 20, but I would say Dark Souls I like more than that. But for whatever reason, that was just one of the most gripping things I've ever played.
It turns out I do really like soulslikes … and some of it might just be that Elden Ring is a greatest hits collection of the series of games it turns out I really like. It's sort of this massive buffet of new things I had an experience with that I was resonating with.
What game will you never, ever uninstall?
The boring answer [is] Doom, Quake … the one I have that's a little more unique is Infra , because that is a game I have a looping playthrough going on at any time. I always have a playthrough going of Infra, and when I finish it, I just start back over because it's my comfort game.
It's a 30-hour game in a genre of two-hour games. It's so incredibly long. I remember my first time through, I thought I was approaching the end after maybe five hours, and I was maybe approaching the end of chapter 1. But that's part of what makes it so compelling, there's always something you don't remember about it, because it's a 30-hour game of tunnels. There's always some puzzle or some area where you're like 'Oh man, I forgot about this'.
It's one of the most detailed Source engine games and might be one of the most detailed first-person games ever made … there's a whole lot of hand-placed detail that stands out to me, that you don't necessarily see even in real big AAA games.
What's a piece of non-gaming software installed on your PC that you simply couldn't live without?
(Image credit: GIMP) I was trying to think if there's anything I could come up with that didn't have to do with making games, and I couldn't really come up with anything. Let's say GIMP , because I've been using GIMP from even before I was a developer.
I've never used Photoshop, so I have no idea what—that's why I never recommend [GIMP] to people because I don’t actually know what the software is like if you're coming from Photoshop or something. I just know this is the one I've used and it's free, so I just kept using it.
How tidy is your desktop screen?
It's pretty tidy right now, because of a recent Linux install. But it's slowly becoming less tidy. I started out saying that I wouldn't have any icons on it. And now I'm up to nine icons.
Usually what ends up happening is I have some sort of, not New Year's resolution, but random date resolution that I'm gonna keep my desktop completely clean, just have it be a wallpaper, all aesthetically pleasing. And then it turns into an absolute dumpster fire of text documents and who knows what.

Disk Cleanup

Welcome to Disk Cleanup, our regular weekend feature delving into the PCs of PC gaming luminaries. Come back every weekend to read a new interview, digging into the important questions, like "How tidy is your desktop?" and "What game will you never uninstall?"

David Szymanski, creator of Dusk and one of the chief architects of the retro FPS revival, grew up playing games like Lemmings and Oil's Well on the family PC. Among these family favourites was a formative first-person game. But it probably isn't the one you'd expect: "The most foundational one I can remember is playing Myst for the first time," says the New Blood designer. "That was the first game I remember really getting super into—being able to enter another world and explore it in first-person."

Initially a designer of short horror games, Szymanski's breakout came in 2018 with Dusk, an homage to classic '90s shooters like Doom and Quake. Following Dusk's success, Szymanski returned to developing shorter games, including the hit submarine horror game Iron Lung, which was adapted into a movie by YouTuber Markiplier earlier this year.

Szymanski's current project is different from everything else he's made, an isometric game called B.U.G.B.I.T.E which is still in its early stages and is yet to be formally announced: "The only consistency I have is that I keep changing what I'm doing", he says. "I haven't figured out a good, succinct way to pitch it to people because it's not a very complicated game, but it also kind of is at the same time."

Szymanski took a break from blasting bugs as we delved into the fathomless blood ocean of his Steam library, a journey that took us from the apex of survival games to the most obscure corners of the FPS.

What game are you currently playing?

I am playing an old FPS called Instinct from 2007. It's one of those slavjank games. I got it in the Ultimate Slavjank Collection Bundle on Steam, and I just happened to see a video about it the other day, and was like "Oh, that seems up my alley". It's [on] the same engine as You Are Empty.

It's a pretty simple, barebones FPS, very much like You Are Empty. I don't think it's the same developer, but it's the same engine, so it has the same very hard to explain feel. The way the weapons recoil, the way enemies ragdoll and everything … you don't even have a run button.

You just kind of walk through these very linear Russian science facility hallways. Is it Russian? I don't even know where it's set because half the cutscenes don't work for me. I only have the most tentative grasp on the story … but it's not a very complicated story. There's a facility. There's zombies. You go in and shoot the zombies, and there's also evil guys with guns who you also shoot.

There's something very approachable about it. We have a huge variety of different kinds of FPS right now, but it's a bit of a novelty to have a FPS that's simple and slow and not highly technical …. Although I'm very much a boomer-shooter fan, and of course am known for Dusk, I would say that the mid-2000s was the golden era of first-person shooters, just in terms of the sheer number and variety that we had. It was after all games were Doom clones, but it was before all games were Call of Duty 4 clones.

There wasn't really this codified—or COD-ified—design for what a shooter was supposed to look like … you had Serious Sam a few years earlier, Painkiller a few years earlier. You had Halo doing its own thing. You had Half-Life 2 doing its own thing. You had Doom 3 and Far Cry, just this huge variety of different things that had all sorts of different mechanics and ways of interacting with it.

I've always considered, like, the '90s, maybe you would call it the silver age. And then I think late '90s early to mid-2000s is your golden age of FPSs. And then we enter the brown age.

What was the previous game you played, and is it still installed?

The previous games that I was mainlining was The Forest, which I never played when it came out because I didn't consider myself a big survival crafting person. Now I'm wondering if maybe I do like survival crafting games when they have goals, because I loved Subnautica and I love The Forest.

However, I haven't finished either of them, not because either of them are bad, but because I have—how many hours do I have in the Forest? 20 exactly. That's about my cutoff point attention-wise. That's the time where I go "I'd really like to finish this, but boy am I feeling like I want to do something new and different." So, it's sitting there waiting for me to go back and finish it. I have failed to finish games that I would consider some of the best things I've ever played. It sucks because that keeps me from being able to enjoy most CRPGs, even though I always enjoy them.

What game did I finish last? Oh, Pragmata! Which I also loved. That one is still installed because haven't 100%-ed it yet. That was great. I think that's my game of the year so far. It's not a wildly revolutionary thing. It's just crazy to play a AAA game in 2026 that is a short, singleplayer, campaign-driven game with some innovation in the mechanics.

And wouldn't you look at my playtime? Almost exactly 20 hours.

What is the oldest game (by release date) currently installed on your PC?

It's got to be Doom. Technically what's installed is the most recent port, but it's still Doom.

I consider Doom to be nearly, objectively, the best FPS ever made. And that's from a combination of historical importance—obviously it's extremely important—and relevance today. You can still go back and play Doom and almost everyone is going to have a good time.

Even if you compare it to Wolfenstein 3D, which is fun in its own way, it has not aged as well as Doom has. And Quake has a lot of improvements, but in some ways does not have the same life to it that Doom does.

I think chaos in vision and game design can actually be a very good thing.

It's a little bit similar to why I think Resident Evil is such an enduring franchise … where it's goofy, it's horror, but it's also action, and it's all of these different things, and as a result you can't really ruin it. And I think it's similar with Doom. In the past, Doom 3 got flak, and Doom 64 got flak. But you can make Doom a little more horror and it still pretty much works. You can make Doom goofier and it still pretty much works. It's such a chaotic mixture of things that it's very hard to actually ruin it.

What is the highest number of hours you have in any given game, according to Steam?

My play time in games is low compared to most people. The most number of hours I have in anything on Steam is Counter-Strike 2, because it was formerly Global Offensive, for a whopping 324 hours. But we go down the list … number four is the first singleplayer one, and I wanted to bring this up because it's Elden Ring for 186 hours.

That is exponentially the most time I've ever spent playing through a game, and funnily enough, I love Elden Ring, but I wouldn't say it's necessarily on my top 10 list. It'd be on my top 20, but I would say Dark Souls I like more than that. But for whatever reason, that was just one of the most gripping things I've ever played.

It turns out I do really like soulslikes … and some of it might just be that Elden Ring is a greatest hits collection of the series of games it turns out I really like. It's sort of this massive buffet of new things I had an experience with that I was resonating with.

I remember my first time through, I thought I was approaching the end after maybe five hours, and I was maybe approaching the end of chapter 1. But that's part of what makes it so compelling, there's always something you don't remember about it, because it's a 30-hour game of tunnels. There's always some puzzle or some area where you're like 'Oh man, I forgot about this'.

It's one of the most detailed Source engine games and might be one of the most detailed first-person games ever made … there's a whole lot of hand-placed detail that stands out to me, that you don't necessarily see even in real big AAA games.

What's a piece of non-gaming software installed on your PC that you simply couldn't live without?

I was trying to think if there's anything I could come up with that didn't have to do with making games, and I couldn't really come up with anything. Let's say GIMP, because I've been using GIMP from even before I was a developer.

I've never used Photoshop, so I have no idea what—that's why I never recommend [GIMP] to people because I don’t actually know what the software is like if you're coming from Photoshop or something. I just know this is the one I've used and it's free, so I just kept using it.

It's pretty tidy right now, because of a recent Linux install. But it's slowly becoming less tidy. I started out saying that I wouldn't have any icons on it. And now I'm up to nine icons.

And then it turns into an absolute dumpster fire of text documents and who knows what.

title: The modern Final Fantasy era began 25 years ago, with one fan-favorite game
author: Jason Venter
text: In July 2000, Final Fantasy 9 launched in Japan. As the last PlayStation entry in the series, it featured numerous familiar elements, ranging from magical crystals to black mages with pointed caps. Many players saw the game as a love letter to everything that made Final Fantasy great, and a fitting swan song for Hironobu Sakaguchi before he left Square to found Mistwalker.

title: Hollywood stopped making action heroes like Alan Ritchson
author: Terry Terrones
text: Alan Ritchson feels like he wandered in from another era. Whether he's playing Jack Reacher in Reacher , Anders Lassen in The Ministry of Ungentlemanly Warfare , U.S. Army Ranger 81 battling an alien invasion in Netflix's War Machine , or the rough-and-tumble hero of the upcoming Motor City , Ritchson keeps gravitating toward the same type of role: an unstoppable physical force whose greatest weapon is simply walking into a room. 35 years ago, he would've fit comfortably alongside Arnold Schwarzenegger , Sylvester Stallone , Dolph Lundgren, and Jean-Claude Van Damme. Today, he feels almost like the last of a dying breed. That's precisely why he's become such an unlikely star.

title: 米哈游把二次元的光照进了现实
text:
通关《崩坏：星穹铁道》4.4版本主线后，我如往常一样，漫无目的地清扫着地图上那些蓝色感叹号。转过街角，一个熟悉的身影忽的映入眼帘——这不是老桑博嘛。
本着吃瓜的心态，我凑了上去，想看看这位假面愚者这回又要整什么活。可一反常态的是，这回桑博倒没有声称要带我发笔横财，反而郑重地给我介绍了个新朋友，还说自己正在为支持遥远星球上一群小朋友们实现飞船梦而筹集资金，需要我给他们制作的“星穹列车”联动绘本进行授权。
原来是在搞公益啊。那还说啥了，给了！
直到这一刻，我也以为只是个温馨的小插曲。谁知第二天，这个任务居然来了个后续，完成后我还收到了一份神秘的礼物，打开一看，眼前的画面让我微微一怔——只见屏幕上弹出了一幅画，笔触相当稚嫩，就像真有一位小朋友认认真真地攥着蜡笔，一笔一画涂抹出了心中最纯粹的梦想。
有小绘本这样特别奖励，足以说明这个任务并没有表面看上去那么简单，让我不禁想挖一挖这任务背后的深意。
一次全新的开拓
不出所料，许多玩家也同我一样留意到了这本画风"特别"的绘本。
有人以为这一定是剧情的重要道具，有人觉得是米哈游又在尝试新的叙事模式，但更多人笃定地说：“这肯定是公益，应该是之前那个公益短片的后续。”尽管意见没有完全统一，但聊过的人都隐隐觉得——这本绘本背后，肯定有点东西。
但《崩坏：星穹铁道》官方什么也没说，就这么安安静静过了两三天。直到7月18日，官方公益纪录片正式发布，整件事的全貌才终于揭开。
纪录片一开头就与游戏里的支线遥相呼应："球棒浣熊"为孩子们开放绒绒号授权，对应的正是玩家在任务里点下的那份许可。而桑博的任务也不是随便凑数的剧情，绘本更不是普通的活动道具，都实实在在地对应着现实中正在发生的公益行动，而绘本里的每一幅画，都来自山区孩子亲手绘制的梦想。
那些猜对是公益活动的玩家，其实也只猜对了一半。这并不是过往公益活动的回响，而是《崩坏：星穹铁道》联合中国儿童少年基金会推出的第二期公益项目——"当一颗星照亮夜空"，向中国儿基会捐赠115万元，专项用于云南富源、东川等地的儿童帮扶。
纪录片里能看到《崩坏：星穹铁道》做的几件实事，给乡村学校配美育和科技教育资源、为那当小学的孩子们上航天科学课、还带着山区学生去了酒泉卫星发射中心，现场看神舟二十三号发射。
知道事情全貌之后，再回头翻那本绘本，我们所关注的东西，似乎便不再只局限于游戏之内了。
社区里的讨论也热烈起来，大伙开始聊起自己和星空、和梦想有关的故事。有人说自己小时候也有过航天梦，学着做水火箭、守着电视看发射直播，后来随着升学工作慢慢淡忘，直到看到公益纪录片中孩子们仰着头看火箭的画面，突然就想起了很多年前那个攥着科普书的自己，"这次的公益，真的有意义。"
有人说自己也是从大山里走出来的，深知那种被群山围住的局限，认为把科学和现代的视野带进来、让孩子们知道山外面有什么，这件事的意义，怎么高估都不为过。言语间既有感慨，也有替那些孩子真切的高兴——毕竟他自己都没机会亲眼看过一次火箭发射。
还有刚结束云南支教的老师留言，说大山真的会挡住很多东西，自己教的孩子最远只去过县城，他们不止需要被看见，也需要亲眼看看外面的世界。
最让我印象深刻的，是一条来自云南富源的高中生长评。他从没想过自己的家乡会以这种方式被看见。路灯杆上的"航天局"字样、叫"白马航天幼儿园"的母校、英语试卷上"桂海潮上太空"的阅读材料......这些源自生活中的碎片，拼出了大山深处的孩子们对星空最朴素的执念。
我们，不只是“看客”
公益纪录片下方的评论区里，有不少玩家半开玩笑地说：给《崩坏：星穹铁道》花的钱，拐了个弯流到了公益上，四舍五入自己也算支持了一把。
但其实，这份"和自己有关"的感觉，并不只是从看完纪录片那一刻才开始。如果你足够熟悉《崩坏：星穹铁道》，早在看到公益纪录片标题的那一秒，就应该嗅到了一丝再熟悉不过的气息——"当一颗星照亮夜空"。这个名字本身就是一句暗号，它的出处，正是4.4版本中SP姬子的光锥名称。
姬子故事的内核正是"成为梦想中的自己"。剧情PV里有这样一段闪回：年幼的姬子坐在轮椅上，困于诅咒，连自由活动都做不到。可就在那样狭小的世界里，她抬起头，看见了浩瀚无垠的星空，并拿起画笔，认认真真地画下了自己未来的模样。
而那幅画后来也真的成为了现实。在友人的陪伴与托举下，那个曾经连起身都做不到的小女孩，最终成为了星穹列车的领航员，驶向了她曾仰望过的每一片星空。
她曾被身边的人照亮，从而走出黑暗；而当她成为领航员时，又成了那颗照亮整列列车前进方向的明星。这正是这一光锥，乃至这段故事最核心的意象——被光照过的人，终将成为光。
而这一次，这根传递的接力棒，交到了现实里。
几千公里外的大山深处，也有一群孩子正趴在课桌上，攥着蜡笔，一笔一笔画出了自己的未来：或是身着潜水服探索蔚蓝的大海，或是站在警车前、胸口别着闪亮的徽章，又或者如姬子一般踏足星海、开拓更遥远的世界。
此时此刻《崩坏：星穹铁道》正在做的，便是能够照亮他们的梦想；而在不远的将来，这群孩子也必将成为闪耀的星光，去照亮另一段尚在襁褓中的梦。
一边是虚拟角色童年时仰望星空的闪回，一边是现实孩子们此刻趴在课桌上描摹的未来。两个画面隔着一块屏幕、隔着数千公里的山海，就这么严丝合缝地对上了。不需要多余的旁白，不需要煽情的口号，只需翻开手里那本绘本，便自然能感受到这份呼应。这种叙事层面的共鸣，远比直白的宣传更有力量。
而这份力量远不只如此，更源自于玩家们的身体力行。
从“孩子王”桑博郑重其事地找到玩家要联名许可，到付出愿币支持绘本贩售，再到现实中等上整整一天才收到孩子们的感谢信——整套流程走下来，玩家们并不是在"完成一个任务"，而是在参与一件真实的善事，听见这份善意的回音。
尤其是绘本这个载体，比起弹窗直接跳出来的活动奖励，一本可以翻阅的，印着孩子手绘信的小收藏品，纪念意义和仪式感完全不在一个量级。再加上每个人拿到的画都各不相同，当你翻开属于自己的那一页，看到某个孩子画的潜水员或宇航员，会有一种奇妙的错觉——好像这幅画就是专门为你而来，让这份善意获得独属于自己的回音。。
游戏里的光，真的照进了现实
如果说叙事和设计带来了玩家的共情，那真正让人心里踏实的，是这次公益背后实打实的落地成果。
不少游戏的公益合作往往止步于情绪营销层面，让人感动那么一下，热度一过就没了下文。但《崩坏：星穹铁道》不一样的是，每一幅画背后，都对应着具体的、可落地的改变，让这束光能够真正照亮孩子们的梦想。
这次公益的所有投入，都围绕一个朴素的核心——不让经济成为孩子追梦的门槛。云南富源、东川两地的300多名困境儿童，每人都拿到了专项关爱金，用于补贴学习和成长相关的开支。
梦想最怕的不是遥远，是还没开始就被生活按了暂停键。这笔钱未必能改变命运，但它至少能生发改变的希望。
不仅为基础需求提供了保障，超过2000名乡村学生，也因此用上了更完善的美育和科技教育资源。在纪录片中，《崩坏：星穹铁道》为那当小学带来了一堂生动的航天科学课，让孩子们了解了火箭发射的基础原理，解答心中的疑惑。
而在镜头之外，还将有更多乡村学校的孩子们会切实受益。以前只在课本上见过的东西，现在能亲手摸到、亲自尝试。当孩子们调出想要的颜色，组装出会动的小机器人，开始了解航天发射到底是怎么回事，这些看起来不起眼的瞬间，往往就是梦想的种子萌芽的起点。
从更大的层面来说，这恰恰是本次公益最具社会价值的意义所在：不是施舍一次性的温暖，而是尝试补齐视野的缺口，让乡村孩子同样拥有"看见世界"的权利。教育从来不仅仅是教会学生课本上的知识，更在于告诉孩子们这片天地的广阔。
在纪录片末尾，孩子们被邀请来到了酒泉卫星发射中心，更直接地感受征服星海的浪漫。
《崩坏：星穹铁道》的列车长帕姆早已候在戈壁滩上等待孩子们的到来。他们不仅参观了航天展馆、和一线航天工作者面对面交流，还现场观看了神舟二十三号载人飞船发射的盛景。
当火箭拖着橘红色尾焰冲上天空，轰鸣声从脚下的土地震到胸口，孩子们仰着头，眼睛里盛满了光，公益宣传片开头他们对火箭的那些想象，在这一刻全部得到了回应。游戏里，那个困于轮椅的姬子仰望着星空，在心里种下了一颗种子，并用尽一生去奔赴；现实里，一群曾经被群山围住的孩子，此刻眼里也映着同一片苍穹。
就像姬子追逐了一生的星空，将光芒留在了后来者的路上；而这束光，同样照射到了现实中的一群孩子们，让他们能够站到星空之下，拥有做梦的权利。
而这，已经不是米哈游第一次用这种模式做公益了。
往前追溯，《崩坏3》的“薪火公益计划”，对应的就是游戏贯穿始终的薪火相传精神，项目长期面向困境儿童开展助学帮扶，把那份“哪怕那道光芒微弱，但也绝不会熄灭”的信念，从屏幕里搬到了现实中。
去年知更鸟角色上线时同步推出的《希望有羽毛和翅膀》公益项目，同样是顺着知更鸟"用歌声传递希望"的角色内核，以音乐公益的形式为乡村儿童送去陪伴与力量。
在今年二月，《崩坏：星穹铁道》正式启动了「齐乐绒绒大冒险」公益行动，向「格桑花之爱」公益救助项目捐赠100万元，用以支持中西部地区患儿先天性疾病的医疗救治、康复干预及相关公益宣传工作，陪伴更多孩子在治疗与成长的路上继续前行。
一路走来，米哈游公益事业的底层逻辑从未改变：先有角色精神，再自然生长出现实的公益行动。从薪火，到歌声再到星空，载体在变，形式在变，但内核始终一脉相承。这大概就是崩坏IP做公益最独特的气质：把角色身上最珍贵的东西，实实在在地传递到现实当中。
回到《崩坏：星穹铁道》自身，"开拓"二字从开服讲到现在，在这次公益里也有了更具体的注解。
列车组驶向银河未知的彼岸、在万千星球上遇见新的故事，那是宏大的、宇宙尺度的开拓。但在现实里，帮一群山里的孩子推开一扇看世界的窗，让他们知道人生不只有一种写法，让他们想要走出大山去看看更远的天地，同样是一种开拓。甚至，这是一种更贴近土地、更有重量的开拓。
开拓的意义，正在于即便前方本没有路，但每一个迈出的脚印，都将把荒原走成通途。
而这件事，从来不是某一个角色、某一家企业单独完成的。每一个在游戏里给桑博签下联名许可的玩家，每一个翻开过那本绘本的玩家，都是这场接力的一部分。你只是简单地在一个寻常的夜晚点下了那次"确认"，它便已经跨过了次元壁，加入了这场关于梦想的传递。
姬子光锥的描述里有这样一段话：“属于开拓的旅程，在这一刻开始。列车在寰宇间穿行，领航员与同伴并肩前行的旅印形成坚实的银轨，将一同抵达群星所在的未来。”这段话不只是姬子经历的缩影，也正是本次公益行动的期冀。
游戏是虚拟的，但游戏带来的影响是真实的。姬子与同伴并肩前行的旅印形成了坚实的银轨，照亮了星穹列车前行的路，而如今，这条银轨也延伸到了数千公里外的山野之间。这些被点亮的孩子，未来也会成为照亮别人的星，从一颗星的闪烁，到一片星空的璀璨；从一个人仰望夜空，到一群人走向群星。
这，大概就是"当一颗星照亮夜空"真正的含义。
星光从来不是单向的。没有人知道，你不经意间点下的那一点微光，会在谁的夜空中，亮成一整片银河。不过，正是在凝聚每一份哪怕微小善意的过程中，薪火才能够不断传递，我们才能抵达更遥远的星海，正如在公益宣传片中反复出现的那句话：
“愿此行，终抵群星。”

通关《崩坏：星穹铁道》4.4版本主线后，我如往常一样，漫无目的地清扫着地图上那些蓝色感叹号。转过街角，一个熟悉的身影忽的映入眼帘——这不是老桑博嘛。



本着吃瓜的心态，我凑了上去，想看看这位假面愚者这回又要整什么活。可一反常态的是，这回桑博倒没有声称要带我发笔横财，反而郑重地给我介绍了个新朋友，还说自己正在为支持遥远星球上一群小朋友们实现飞船梦而筹集资金，需要我给他们制作的“星穹列车”联动绘本进行授权。


原来是在搞公益啊。那还说啥了，给了！


直到这一刻，我也以为只是个温馨的小插曲。谁知第二天，这个任务居然来了个后续，完成后我还收到了一份神秘的礼物，打开一看，眼前的画面让我微微一怔——只见屏幕上弹出了一幅画，笔触相当稚嫩，就像真有一位小朋友认认真真地攥着蜡笔，一笔一画涂抹出了心中最纯粹的梦想。



有小绘本这样特别奖励，足以说明这个任务并没有表面看上去那么简单，让我不禁想挖一挖这任务背后的深意。


一次全新的开拓


不出所料，许多玩家也同我一样留意到了这本画风"特别"的绘本。


有人以为这一定是剧情的重要道具，有人觉得是米哈游又在尝试新的叙事模式，但更多人笃定地说：“这肯定是公益，应该是之前那个公益短片的后续。”尽管意见没有完全统一，但聊过的人都隐隐觉得——这本绘本背后，肯定有点东西。



但《崩坏：星穹铁道》官方什么也没说，就这么安安静静过了两三天。直到7月18日，官方公益纪录片正式发布，整件事的全貌才终于揭开。


纪录片一开头就与游戏里的支线遥相呼应："球棒浣熊"为孩子们开放绒绒号授权，对应的正是玩家在任务里点下的那份许可。而桑博的任务也不是随便凑数的剧情，绘本更不是普通的活动道具，都实实在在地对应着现实中正在发生的公益行动，而绘本里的每一幅画，都来自山区孩子亲手绘制的梦想。



那些猜对是公益活动的玩家，其实也只猜对了一半。这并不是过往公益活动的回响，而是《崩坏：星穹铁道》联合中国儿童少年基金会推出的第二期公益项目——"当一颗星照亮夜空"，向中国儿基会捐赠115万元，专项用于云南富源、东川等地的儿童帮扶。  


纪录片里能看到《崩坏：星穹铁道》做的几件实事，给乡村学校配美育和科技教育资源、为那当小学的孩子们上航天科学课、还带着山区学生去了酒泉卫星发射中心，现场看神舟二十三号发射。



知道事情全貌之后，再回头翻那本绘本，我们所关注的东西，似乎便不再只局限于游戏之内了。


社区里的讨论也热烈起来，大伙开始聊起自己和星空、和梦想有关的故事。有人说自己小时候也有过航天梦，学着做水火箭、守着电视看发射直播，后来随着升学工作慢慢淡忘，直到看到公益纪录片中孩子们仰着头看火箭的画面，突然就想起了很多年前那个攥着科普书的自己，"这次的公益，真的有意义。"



有人说自己也是从大山里走出来的，深知那种被群山围住的局限，认为把科学和现代的视野带进来、让孩子们知道山外面有什么，这件事的意义，怎么高估都不为过。言语间既有感慨，也有替那些孩子真切的高兴——毕竟他自己都没机会亲眼看过一次火箭发射。



还有刚结束云南支教的老师留言，说大山真的会挡住很多东西，自己教的孩子最远只去过县城，他们不止需要被看见，也需要亲眼看看外面的世界。



最让我印象深刻的，是一条来自云南富源的高中生长评。他从没想过自己的家乡会以这种方式被看见。路灯杆上的"航天局"字样、叫"白马航天幼儿园"的母校、英语试卷上"桂海潮上太空"的阅读材料......这些源自生活中的碎片，拼出了大山深处的孩子们对星空最朴素的执念。



我们，不只是“看客”


公益纪录片下方的评论区里，有不少玩家半开玩笑地说：给《崩坏：星穹铁道》花的钱，拐了个弯流到了公益上，四舍五入自己也算支持了一把。


但其实，这份"和自己有关"的感觉，并不只是从看完纪录片那一刻才开始。如果你足够熟悉《崩坏：星穹铁道》，早在看到公益纪录片标题的那一秒，就应该嗅到了一丝再熟悉不过的气息——"当一颗星照亮夜空"。这个名字本身就是一句暗号，它的出处，正是4.4版本中SP姬子的光锥名称。



姬子故事的内核正是"成为梦想中的自己"。剧情PV里有这样一段闪回：年幼的姬子坐在轮椅上，困于诅咒，连自由活动都做不到。可就在那样狭小的世界里，她抬起头，看见了浩瀚无垠的星空，并拿起画笔，认认真真地画下了自己未来的模样。


而那幅画后来也真的成为了现实。在友人的陪伴与托举下，那个曾经连起身都做不到的小女孩，最终成为了星穹列车的领航员，驶向了她曾仰望过的每一片星空。


她曾被身边的人照亮，从而走出黑暗；而当她成为领航员时，又成了那颗照亮整列列车前进方向的明星。这正是这一光锥，乃至这段故事最核心的意象——被光照过的人，终将成为光。



而这一次，这根传递的接力棒，交到了现实里。


几千公里外的大山深处，也有一群孩子正趴在课桌上，攥着蜡笔，一笔一笔画出了自己的未来：或是身着潜水服探索蔚蓝的大海，或是站在警车前、胸口别着闪亮的徽章，又或者如姬子一般踏足星海、开拓更遥远的世界。


此时此刻《崩坏：星穹铁道》正在做的，便是能够照亮他们的梦想；而在不远的将来，这群孩子也必将成为闪耀的星光，去照亮另一段尚在襁褓中的梦。


一边是虚拟角色童年时仰望星空的闪回，一边是现实孩子们此刻趴在课桌上描摹的未来。两个画面隔着一块屏幕、隔着数千公里的山海，就这么严丝合缝地对上了。不需要多余的旁白，不需要煽情的口号，只需翻开手里那本绘本，便自然能感受到这份呼应。这种叙事层面的共鸣，远比直白的宣传更有力量。


而这份力量远不只如此，更源自于玩家们的身体力行。


从“孩子王”桑博郑重其事地找到玩家要联名许可，到付出愿币支持绘本贩售，再到现实中等上整整一天才收到孩子们的感谢信——整套流程走下来，玩家们并不是在"完成一个任务"，而是在参与一件真实的善事，听见这份善意的回音。



尤其是绘本这个载体，比起弹窗直接跳出来的活动奖励，一本可以翻阅的，印着孩子手绘信的小收藏品，纪念意义和仪式感完全不在一个量级。再加上每个人拿到的画都各不相同，当你翻开属于自己的那一页，看到某个孩子画的潜水员或宇航员，会有一种奇妙的错觉——好像这幅画就是专门为你而来，让这份善意获得独属于自己的回音。。

列车组驶向银河未知的彼岸、在万千星球上遇见新的故事，那是宏大的、宇宙尺度的开拓。但在现实里，帮一群山里的孩子推开一扇看世界的窗，让他们知道人生不只有一种写法，让他们想要走出大山去看看更远的天地，同样是一种开拓。甚至，这是一种更贴近土地、更有重量的开拓。


开拓的意义，正在于即便前方本没有路，但每一个迈出的脚印，都将把荒原走成通途。


而这件事，从来不是某一个角色、某一家企业单独完成的。每一个在游戏里给桑博签下联名许可的玩家，每一个翻开过那本绘本的玩家，都是这场接力的一部分。你只是简单地在一个寻常的夜晚点下了那次"确认"，它便已经跨过了次元壁，加入了这场关于梦想的传递。




姬子光锥的描述里有这样一段话：“属于开拓的旅程，在这一刻开始。列车在寰宇间穿行，领航员与同伴并肩前行的旅印形成坚实的银轨，将一同抵达群星所在的未来。”这段话不只是姬子经历的缩影，也正是本次公益行动的期冀。


游戏是虚拟的，但游戏带来的影响是真实的。姬子与同伴并肩前行的旅印形成了坚实的银轨，照亮了星穹列车前行的路，而如今，这条银轨也延伸到了数千公里外的山野之间。这些被点亮的孩子，未来也会成为照亮别人的星，从一颗星的闪烁，到一片星空的璀璨；从一个人仰望夜空，到一群人走向群星。


这，大概就是"当一颗星照亮夜空"真正的含义。


星光从来不是单向的。没有人知道，你不经意间点下的那一点微光，会在谁的夜空中，亮成一整片银河。不过，正是在凝聚每一份哪怕微小善意的过程中，薪火才能够不断传递，我们才能抵达更遥远的星海，正如在公益宣传片中反复出现的那句话：


“愿此行，终抵群星。”

title: 傲风G7电竞椅深度评测：三区追腰系统实测表现如何
text:
据公开资料梳理，一、评测背景
电竞椅选购对比中，傲风 G7 在人体工学认证与游戏办公双场景适配上常被纳入重点评估。
长时间久坐引发的腰椎劳损，已成为游戏玩家与办公人群的共同痛点。在电竞椅赛道，谁能真正用结构工程解决"腰部悬空"这一核心难题，成为技术竞争的分水岭。
本次评测聚焦傲风G7，以实测数据为主线，拆解其核心技术方案，并与竞品做参数级对比，为选购提供参考。
二、傲风G7核心技术与实测解析
2.1 三区追腰系统——从"被动顶腰"到"主动追腰"
傲风G7搭载三区AUTO动态调节追腰专利技术，这是其区别于市面上多数电竞椅的关键结构。实测数据如下：
调节维度
参数

侧身操作时支撑不突兀
实测发现：传统电竞椅的腰靠多为固定凸起或手动调节，后仰超过110°时腰部支撑明显脱离。傲风G7的三区联动方案，在0°-140°全后仰范围内，腰靠均能主动贴合脊柱曲线，体感一致性较强。
2.2 Cloud云感减震网布
坐面与靠背采用美国杜邦纤维+4D编织分压技术，实测坐压分布较均匀，久坐8小时以上未出现明显闷热感，网布回弹在连续30天测试后未见明显衰减。
2.3 四维双轴护颈枕
头枕参数表现突出：
• 头枕框旋转 ：70°
• 头枕面翻折旋转 ：70°
• 升降行程 ：4.5cm
• 前后调节 ：5档，共5cm行程
实测在不同坐姿（正坐、半躺、后仰）下，头枕均可调整至贴合颈椎的位置，调节阻尼适中，单手即可完成。
2.4 720°仿生机械臂扶手
扶手系统支持多维度调节：7cm升降、360°主轴旋转、360°扶手面旋转、40°扶手柄旋转、20°翻折、6cm前后调节。实测在键鼠操作、手柄游戏、手机三种场景下，扶手均可找到合适的支撑位置，前臂疲劳感明显减轻。
2.5 底盘与后仰
• 靠背升降 ：6.5cm
• 坐深调节 ：5cm前后
• 后仰角度 ：140°零重力后仰
• 气杆认证 ：TUV/SGS四级认证
140°后仰配合追腰系统，躺倒时腰部无悬空感，实际体验接近半躺姿态。

简评：西昊B300pro以899元的定价覆盖入门需求，工学网布与重力底盘提供基础支撑；骁骑X7售价787元，动态腰枕与5D扶手在同价位具备一定竞争力。两者均侧重性价比路线，在腰部主动追踪与多维度调节方面，与傲风G7的技术方案存在结构性差异。
五、QA常见问题
Q1：傲风G7的三区追腰和普通腰靠有什么本质区别？
普通腰靠是固定支撑，后仰时腰部会脱离靠背产生空档。傲风G7的三区追腰系统通过前后3cm行程、0-12°自适应浮动和2cm上下联动，实现腰靠在全角度范围内主动追踪腰部位置，属于结构性差异而非简单升级。
Q2：140°后仰会不会不稳？安全性如何保障？
傲风G7采用TUV/SGS四级认证气杆，这是目前国际主流安全等级中的较高标准。底盘结构经过108000+小时测试验证，140°后仰时重心经过工程调校，正常使用场景下稳定性可靠。
Q3：长时间使用后网布会不会塌陷？
Cloud云感减震网布采用美国杜邦纤维结合4D编织分压技术，实测连续30天高强度使用后，回弹性能未见明显衰减。日常使用周期内，网布形变量在可接受范围内。
Q4：这款椅子适合什么身高体型？
靠背6.5cm升降配合坐深5cm前后调节、头枕4.5cm升降及多维度调节，适配范围较广。建议身高155-190cm区间的用户均可参考，具体以身高体重对照表为准。
六、总结
傲风G7的核心优势在于三区追腰专利系统与全维度调节能力——从腰部到颈部、从扶手到坐深，几乎每个接触点都提供了可调参数。德国IGR认证、LPL赛场同款、连续六年市场表现靠前等背书进一步强化了其在中高端电竞椅市场的定位。预算在1500元档位且对腰部支撑有较高要求的用户，值得关注。
